"Incommensurable" describes two (or more) things that share no common measure — no single yardstick, scale, or standard exists that can meaningfully measure, compare, or rank both of them together.

The opposite word is "commensurable," which means that a common measure does exist. Keeping that contrast in mind will help everything below click into place.
The Mathematical Meaning (Its Original, Precise Sense)

This is where the word was born, and understanding it here gives you the sharpest possible grip on the concept.

Two quantities are mathematically incommensurable if there is no unit of measurement — no matter how tiny you make it — that can fit into both of them a perfect, whole number of times.

Here's a concrete example. Take a square whose sides are exactly 1 unit long. Now draw a line diagonally across it from one corner to the opposite corner. That diagonal has a length of √2, which is approximately 1.41421356... and the decimal never ends and never falls into a repeating pattern.

Now ask yourself: is there any unit of length, however fine, that divides evenly into both 1 (the side) and √2 (the diagonal) with no remainder? The answer is no — there is no such unit. You can make your measuring unit as small as you want, and it will always divide cleanly into one of them but leave a leftover with the other. These two lengths are therefore incommensurable with each other.

Contrast this with two lengths like 6 cm and 9 cm. These are commensurable because a 3 cm unit fits into 6 cm exactly twice, and into 9 cm exactly three times — a single common unit works for both. Their relationship can be expressed as a clean ratio of whole numbers (6:9, or simplified, 2:3). With √2 and 1, no such clean ratio is possible.

This discovery was historically enormous. Ancient Greek mathematicians assumed that any two lengths could always be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers. The diagonal of the unit square shattered that assumption. The two lengths belong to fundamentally different numerical worlds, and no bridge of a common unit can span them.
The Broader Meaning (Philosophical and Everyday Use)

The word has grown well beyond mathematics and is now used in philosophy, ethics, science, and everyday language to describe situations where two things are so different in nature or kind that no shared scale can place them side by side and rank them.

This is a powerful idea. A few examples will make it vivid:

Values you can't weigh against each other. Suppose someone asks you: "Which matters more — personal freedom or equality?" Many philosophers argue these two values are incommensurable. It's not that they're equal, and it's not that we simply haven't thought hard enough. It's that freedom and equality belong to different categories of value. There is no single "moral importance meter" on which you can place both and read off which one scores higher. You can care deeply about both, but the idea of converting them into a single currency for comparison breaks down.

A human life versus money. Governments sometimes face decisions like: "Should we spend $100 million to redesign this highway and prevent an estimated three deaths per year?" Some people feel deeply that a human life and a sum of money are incommensurable — they are not just different in quantity but different in kind, and placing them on the same scale does violence to what a human life is. Whether or not you agree, this captures exactly what the word is pointing at.

Two scientific worldviews. The philosopher Thomas Kuhn argued that when science undergoes a revolution — for example, the shift from Newtonian physics to Einstein's theory of relativity — the two frameworks are incommensurable. They don't merely disagree on the answers; they use different concepts, define their key terms differently, and aren't even asking exactly the same questions. There is no shared neutral language in which you can directly translate one into the other and compare them cleanly. It's not a small gap — it's a gap in the very architecture of how each framework sees the world.
A Crucial Distinction: Incommensurable Is Not the Same as Incomparable

These two words are easy to confuse, but there is an important difference.

Something is incomparable when you can't rank it against something else — but this might simply be because you don't have enough information, or you haven't tried hard enough, or the comparison is very difficult. The impossibility is practical and potentially fixable.

Something is incommensurable when the impossibility of comparison runs deeper: no common standard of measurement exists in principle. It's not a gap in effort or information. It's a gap built into the very nature of the things being compared. They belong to different categories that don't share a common axis.

Think of it this way: two paintings might be hard to compare in quality — that makes them difficult to rank, but not necessarily incommensurable. But comparing the height of a painting against the beauty of a painting — those two attributes have no common scale at all. Height is measured in centimeters; beauty is not. They are incommensurable.
Another Crucial Distinction: Incommensurable Does Not Mean "Equal"

This is a subtle trap. When people hear that two things can't be compared, they often assume it means they must be equal in value or importance. That is wrong.

When two things are incommensurable, the concepts of "greater than," "less than," and "equal to" simply do not apply. Not because they happen to land at the same point on a scale, but because there is no scale on which to place them in the first place. Saying they're "equal" would itself require a common measure — which is precisely what's missing.
How the Word Is Typically Used

You will almost always see it in one of these patterns:

  • "X and Y are incommensurable."
  • "X is incommensurable with Y."
  • "These two things are incommensurable in value / by any standard measure."

• "For many people, the grief of losing a child and the satisfaction of career success are incommensurable — no scale can weigh one against the other."
  • "In mathematics, the side and the diagonal of a square are incommensurable quantities."
  • "The two rival theories were incommensurable: they didn't just give different answers, they asked fundamentally different questions."
  • "She felt the decision was impossible — not because the options were equally good, but because they were incommensurable, each valuable in a way the other simply wasn't."
  • "Economic growth and ecological health may be incommensurable values, which is why policy debates about them so often feel like talking past each other."

The word "incommensurable" is a precise way of saying: these two things don't fit on the same ruler. In mathematics, this is about the absence of a common unit of measurement. In philosophy and everyday life, it's about the absence of a common scale of value, importance, or meaning. In both cases, the core claim is the same — not that comparison is hard, not that we haven't tried, but that the very idea of a shared measure breaks down at a fundamental level.
